summary: Describes an Extensible Provisioning Protocol extension for managing domain names subject to grace period policies defined by ICANN. Grace periods let some registry actions be reversed or otherwise handled for a time.

eli5.summary: If you register a domain by mistake, there is a short window to undo it. This document says how the system handles that window.

questions: what is the redemption grace period
how to restore a deleted domain with epp
what is an epp restore report
subtitle: How registrars restore a deleted domain name during the redemption grace period, and how grace periods show up in EPP.

tldr.problem: ICANN grace period policies let some domain actions be reversed for a short time, but the base EPP domain mapping has no way to show grace period status or to ask for a deleted domain to be restored.
tldr.mechanism: This XML extension adds an rgpStatus element to EPP domain info responses and a restore element to the EPP domain update command, plus a restore report that the registrar sends to prove the restore was legitimate.
tldr.outcome: A deleted domain can move through redemptionPeriod and pendingRestore back to its prior state, or on to pendingDelete and a purge. Other grace periods (add, auto-renew, renew, transfer) are exposed as status values.

today: RFC 3915 is a Proposed Standard from October 2004. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is an extension of the EPP domain name mapping in RFC 3731.

sections.title: Grace Periods and This Extension
sections.content:
This document defines an extension of the EPP domain name mapping (RFC 3731) for version 1.0 of the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP, RFC 3730). It is specified in XML and XML Schema.

ICANN developed a proposal during 2002 for a "grace period" for domain name recovery (redemption) before a name is purged from the registry. This mapping extends the EPP domain <update> command to start redemption for a name that has entered the Redemption Grace Period (RGP), and extends the domain <info> response to show the grace period status of a domain.

A March 2003 ICANN task force report described other grace periods too, and the extension names them as status values. The length of each grace period is registry operational policy and is not addressed here.
sections.eli5: When a domain is deleted or renewed there is a short waiting time where mistakes can be fixed. This document gives those waiting times names a computer can read, and a way to undo a deletion.

sections.title: The Grace Period Status Values
sections.content:
Seven new status values describe where a domain is in grace period processing.

  • addPeriod: after the initial registration. If the registrar deletes the name now, the registry credits the registrar for the registration cost.
  • autoRenewPeriod: after a registration period expires and the registry renews it automatically. Deleting the name earns a credit for the renewal.
  • renewPeriod: after the registrar explicitly renews the name. Deleting earns a credit for the renewal.
  • transferPeriod: after sponsorship moves from one registrar to another. If the new registrar deletes the name, it gets a credit for the transfer.
  • redemptionPeriod: a <delete> was received but the domain is not purged yet, so the deletion can still be aborted by a restore.
  • pendingRestore: the domain is being restored after being in redemptionPeriod.
  • pendingDelete: purge processing has started after redemption. The domain MUST also be in the EPP domain mapping's pendingDelete status.
sections.eli5: Each waiting time gets a name tag, like "just signed up", "just renewed", "in the recycling bin" and "being taken out of the bin".

sections.title: The Redemption Grace Period Flow
sections.content:
A domain starts in EPP status ok (or another status that allows <delete>). Once a <delete> is processed successfully, the EPP status becomes pendingDelete and the RGP status becomes redemptionPeriod. It stays there until a <restore> is requested or the redemption period elapses.

If a restore request succeeds, the RGP status becomes pendingRestore, and the registry waits, for a period it defines, for a restore report from the registrar. If no report arrives, the domain returns to the redemption period state. If a report arrives, the EPP status returns to ok (or what it was before the delete) and the RGP status is removed.

If the redemption period passes with no restore request, the RGP status becomes pendingDelete for a registry-defined period. The name is then purged and becomes available for re-registration. The RFC notes that restore reports can also be delivered out of band, for example on a web site.
sections.eli5: Deleting a domain puts it in a bin for a while. The owner's registrar can ask to take it back and must send a note explaining why. If nobody does, the bin is emptied and anyone can sign up for the name.

sections.title: Commands: Info and Update
sections.content:
The extension adds nothing to the EPP <check>, <create>, <delete>, <renew> or <transfer> commands. It changes two things.

First, a successful <info> response MUST include an <extension> element holding an <rgp:infData> element, which contains an <rgp:rgpStatus> element with an s attribute naming the current grace period status.

Second, the domain <update> command can carry an <rgp:update> extension with an <rgp:restore> element. Its required op attribute is either request (no report; an <rgp:report> MUST NOT be present) or report (a report MUST be present). A report may be submitted more than once if corrections are needed. Because redemption must not change the domain itself, at least one empty <domain:add>, <domain:rem> or <domain:chg> element MUST be present. A successful restore request gets a response with an <rgp:upData> whose status is pendingRestore. A successful report gets a normal response with no extension, since accepting the report completes the process.
sections.eli5: Asking for a domain's status adds one extra line saying which waiting time it is in. Asking to restore is a normal update message with an extra "please restore" box, and later a second one with the explanation attached.

sections.title: The Restore Report
sections.content:
The restore report (<rgp:report>) proves the restore is legitimate. It contains:

  • <rgp:preData>: the registration data from before the delete.
  • <rgp:postData>: the registration data at the time of the report.
  • <rgp:delTime> and <rgp:resTime>: when the delete request and the original restore request were sent.
  • <rgp:resReason>: a brief reason for restoring.
  • Two <rgp:statement> elements: one that the registrar has not restored the name to use or sell it for itself or a third party, and one that the report is factual to the best of its knowledge.
  • An optional <rgp:other> element with supporting information.

Registration data and statements have no required format; free text and XML are both allowed, and English is the default language for statements (an optional lang attribute can say otherwise). Dates and times MUST be UTC in the extended form of RFC 3339 with upper case T and Z. More detail on what a report must contain is available from ICANN, according to the RFC.
sections.eli5: To get the domain back, the registrar fills in a form: what the domain looked like before, what it looks like now, when things happened, why, and a promise that it is not a sneaky grab for the name.

sections.title: Security and Registration
sections.content:
The extension provides no security services beyond those of EPP, the EPP domain mapping and the layers beneath them, and their security considerations apply here too. In addition, restoring a deleted domain MUST be restricted to the sponsoring client, authenticated by the mechanisms in RFC 3730. Any other client's attempt MUST be rejected with an appropriate EPP authorization error.

The extension is identified by the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:rgp-1.0 and the schema urn:ietf:params:xml:schema:rgp-1.0, both registered with IANA. The RFC also says the extension inherits the internationalization conventions of the domain mapping, and recommends UTF-8.
sections.eli5: Only the registrar that looks after the domain may ask to take it out of the bin. Anyone else is told no.

items.label: Transfer grace period
items.desc: After sponsorship moves to another registrar.

items.label: Redemption period
items.desc: Deleted but not purged; can be restored.

items.desc: Being restored; awaiting the restore report.

items.desc: Purge processing after redemption has run out.
